reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ATS-ERS
clinicalPearls: A rare syndrome classically defined by a triad of yellow, thickened, slow-growing nails, lymphoedema, and respiratory manifestations, though not all three are present in every patient
The characteristic nails are yellow to greenish, over-curved, thickened, and grow very slowly, often with loss of the cuticle and lunula
Respiratory features include recurrent pleural effusions (frequently chylous), chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and recurrent respiratory infections
The pleural effusions are typically exudative and often lymphocyte-rich or chylous, reflecting impaired lymphatic drainage
Most cases occur in middle-aged or older adults and the disorder is usually acquired rather than inherited
It has been associated with malignancy, immunodeficiency, and autoimmune disease, so a search for an underlying condition is warranted
Management is largely supportive - drainage of symptomatic effusions, treatment of infections and bronchiectasis, and nail care - as no specific cure exists
Nail changes and other features may partially improve if an associated condition is treated, and vitamin E and other measures have been tried with variable results
reference.pathophysiology: Yellow nail syndrome is thought to arise from functional or structural abnormality of the lymphatic system, producing impaired lymphatic drainage that underlies the lymphoedema, chylous pleural effusions, and slow, discoloured nail growth. Microlymphatic dysfunction and, in some accounts, associated microvascular changes lead to protein-rich fluid accumulation in the pleural space and peripheral tissues. Recurrent sinopulmonary infection and bronchiectasis may reflect both impaired lymphatic clearance and, in some patients, coexisting immune dysfunction. The condition may be idiopathic or associated with malignancy, autoimmune disease, or immunodeficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Onychomycosis and other primary nail disorders
Other causes of chylous or lymphocytic pleural effusion
Primary and secondary lymphoedema of other cause
Bronchiectasis and chronic rhinosinusitis from other aetiologies
Nail changes of psoriasis or chronic systemic disease
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of the nail, lymphatic, and respiratory triad
Pleural fluid analysis to characterise effusions as exudative, lymphocytic, or chylous
High-resolution CT to assess for bronchiectasis and sinus disease
Immunological evaluation where recurrent infection suggests immunodeficiency
Age-appropriate screening for underlying malignancy or autoimmune disease
redFlags: Large or rapidly reaccumulating pleural effusion causing respiratory compromise
Features suggesting an underlying malignancy driving the syndrome
Severe or recurrent respiratory infection with clinical deterioration
Progressive bronchiectasis with declining respiratory function
reference.prognosis: The syndrome tends to be chronic; nail changes may fluctuate or occasionally resolve spontaneously, and prognosis is largely determined by the burden of respiratory disease and any associated underlying condition.
pitfalls: Treating discoloured nails as simple fungal infection and missing the wider syndrome
Failing to investigate recurrent pleural effusions for their chylous or lymphatic nature
Not searching for an associated malignancy, autoimmune disease, or immunodeficiency
Overlooking bronchiectasis as a treatable contributor to recurrent infection
